lines.text: Imagine you wake up tomorrow, check your bank account, and there it is: one million dollars.
And not just for you. Your neighbor got it. Your boss got it. The barista at your favorite coffee shop got it too. Every single person on Earth.
No catch, no taxes, no strings attached. Just one million dollars, for everyone, at exactly the same moment.
Sounds like the end of all money problems, right? Today we play it through, step by step, with real numbers.
And spoiler: by the end of this video, you will see why free money for everyone might be one of the most expensive ideas ever.
Phase one: how much money is that, actually?
There are roughly eight point two billion people living on this planet right now.
One million dollars each adds up to about eight point two quadrillion dollars. That is an eight, followed by fifteen zeros.
Or put differently: if you spent one million dollars every single day, you would need about twenty-two million years to spend it all.
For comparison: everything the whole world produces in one year, every car, every meal, every haircut, is worth roughly one hundred and fifteen trillion dollars.
And all the wealth on Earth combined, every house, every company and every bank account, is estimated at around four hundred and fifty trillion dollars.
So this new money would be more than seventy times the yearly world economy, and roughly eighteen times everything humanity owns.
Even all the US dollars that exist today, as cash and in bank accounts, add up to only around twenty-two trillion dollars.
That money does not come from somewhere. It has to be created out of thin air. And that is the first crack in the dream.
Phase two: day one, the party.
On day one, it feels incredible. Credit cards, student loans and mortgages are paid off with one click.
People book vacations, order new phones and finally buy the car they always dreamed about.
Restaurants are booked out for weeks. Car dealers sell their entire lots in a single weekend.
And quite a few people walk into the office, smile, and quit on the spot.
Online shops crash under the traffic. Orders shoot up like never before.
For a few days, everyone feels like a lottery winner. Because, in a way, everyone is one.
But here is the catch. The number of cars, phones and plane seats did not change overnight. Only the amount of money did.
Phase three: prices explode.
When a lot more money chases the same amount of stuff, sellers do the obvious thing. They raise their prices.
Think of it like an auction. If everyone in the room suddenly has a million more, the painting does not get any better. The bids just get bigger.
A coffee that cost four dollars yesterday could cost forty dollars next week. And four hundred a few weeks later.
Rents and house prices jump too, because everybody wants a bigger place at the same time, but there are not more homes.
Shops would have to change their price tags several times a day just to keep up.
And the things everyone needs most, like food, housing and energy, usually get more expensive first, because nobody can do without them.
Economists call this inflation. And when it spins completely out of control, they call it hyperinflation.
This is not just a thought experiment. It has happened before, and it went very badly.
Phase four: history already tried it.
In Germany in nineteen twenty-three, at the peak, prices roughly doubled every three to four days.
Workers were paid once or even twice a day, and rushed to spend their wages, because money lost value by the hour.
Photos from that time show children playing with bundles of banknotes, because the paper was worth more as a toy than as money.
In Zimbabwe in two thousand eight, at the worst point, prices doubled about every single day.
And in Hungary in nineteen forty-six, it was even more extreme. Prices doubled about every fifteen hours. That is still the worst case ever recorded.
The country eventually printed a one hundred trillion dollar note. Within months, it was close to worthless.
In both cases, there was suddenly much more money, but not more stuff to buy with it.
Germany only got out by introducing a new currency. One new mark was exchanged for one trillion old marks.
Phase five: who still goes to work?
Now the big question. With a million dollars in your account, would you still go to work tomorrow morning?
Research gives us a hint. In Sweden, economists followed thousands of people who won large lottery prizes.
Most winners kept working. They cut back only a little: for every hundred dollars they won, they earned about one dollar less per year.
But those were a few lucky winners in a normal economy. If everyone gets the million at the same time, the math changes completely.
If prices rise tenfold, your million suddenly buys what a hundred thousand used to. And many people would need their jobs again.
In the meantime, some jobs become hard to fill. Cleaners, delivery drivers, nurses on the night shift.
And who still harvests the food, drives the trucks and repairs the power lines? If fewer people do that work, there is even less stuff to buy.
Imagine a hospital where half the staff stays home for a month. Or a supermarket where nobody restocks the shelves anymore.
Less supply, while demand explodes. For prices, that is the worst possible combination.
So businesses have to pay a lot more to find workers. And that pushes prices up even further.
Phase six: winners and losers.
Not everyone loses in this world. The biggest winners are people with large debts.
If you owe two hundred thousand dollars on your house, you pay it off in a second. The debt does not grow with inflation.
Banks, on the other hand, lose. The loans they handed out are paid back with money that is suddenly worth much less.
The biggest losers are savers. Someone who saved half a million over thirty years now has the same as everyone else, and their savings melt every day.
People who own real things, like houses, land or companies, often do better, because those prices tend to rise with inflation.
So the gap between rich and poor would not disappear. It would just get reshuffled.
Phase seven: where it ends.
After a few months, the million is worth only a fraction of what it was on day one.
Everyone is a millionaire. And that is exactly why being a millionaire suddenly means almost nothing.
Prices settle at a much higher level, and most people end up not much richer than before.
Some are even poorer, because their savings and fixed incomes, like pensions, lost most of their value.
In the end, the government would probably have to do what Germany did: create a new currency and cut off a few zeros, just to make prices readable again.
Contracts, wages and savings plans would all have to be renegotiated. For years, nobody would really know what anything is worth.
Phase eight: the real lesson.
Money is not wealth by itself. It is a ticket you trade for real things: food, homes, haircuts and time.
Real wealth comes from what people build and produce. More bread, more houses, better tools and smarter ideas.
Think about it: if printing money alone made people rich, every poor country could simply print its way out of poverty. None ever has.
If you print money faster than the economy grows, you do not create wealth. You just cut the same cake into more slices.
That is why central banks are so careful about how much new money they create.
Smaller cash payments work very differently. Alaska pays residents a yearly dividend from oil money, usually in the low thousands of dollars.
Studies found it did not reduce employment overall. So the size matters. A little extra money can help. A million for everyone breaks the system.
Even much smaller waves of new money can push up prices, if they arrive faster than the economy can produce more goods.
Phase nine: the honest answer.
So, would a million for everyone make us all rich? No. It would make us all millionaires. And that is not the same thing.
What actually makes a society richer is producing more and better things. And for you personally, the lesson is simple.
Your own million does not come from a money printer. It comes from earning, saving, investing, and above all, time.
Now tell me: what would you do with a million dollars, if only you got it? Write it in the comments.
And subscribe for more honest money math. In the next video, we look at why prices almost never go back down.
